records.sourceFile: A mechanistic approach to blood flow occlusion.pdf

paper.citation: Loenneke JP, Wilson GJ, Wilson JM. A mechanistic approach to blood flow occlusion. Int J Sports Med 2010;31:1-4.
paper.abstract: This narrative review describes the proposed mechanisms by which low-intensity blood flow occlusion training may increase skeletal muscle hypertrophy. The mechanisms covered are metabolite accumulation and growth hormone, fast-twitch fibre recruitment, mTOR signalling, heat shock proteins, nitric oxide synthase-1 and myostatin. The authors conclude that the supporting research is incomplete.
paper.tldr: Low-load occlusion training (as low as 20% 1RM with moderate occlusion) is proposed to build muscle through several mechanisms. The authors describe the evidence for each as incomplete, so treat them as hypotheses rather than established causes.
paper.methods: Narrative review of the literature on blood flow occlusion and muscle growth, organised by proposed mechanism. The article does not describe a systematic search or appraisal of study quality.
paper.findings: The review reports that occlusion raises blood, plasma and muscle lactate and growth hormone, with one study showing a growth hormone rise about 290 times baseline. It also cites a threefold rise in S6K1 phosphorylation immediately after occlusion exercise. The authors state that the link between lactate and growth hormone is unclear and that the mechanisms remain unproven.
paper.limitations: The review has no search strategy and no quality appraisal. Several key mechanistic findings come from animal studies, and the authors call for human studies to confirm the heat shock protein findings of Kawada and Ishii. The review does not compare occlusion training directly with heavy resistance training.
paper.practicalImplications: Low-load occlusion training (about 20% 1RM with moderate occlusion, around 100 mmHg) is presented as an option for people who cannot tolerate heavy loading. Staff should not use any single proposed pathway, such as growth hormone, to predict hypertrophy outcomes.
paper.athleteDev: The review describes low-load occlusion training as a hypertrophy option and states it may benefit athletes. Because the mechanisms are unproven, it does not show that occlusion training is superior to conventional heavy resistance training for athletes.
paper.rtp: The review mentions possible benefits in ACL rehabilitation, cardiac rehabilitation and post-operative patients but calls for more research. It contains no return-to-sport criteria and no data on re-injury, so it cannot inform return-to-sport decisions.

records.sourceFile: A review of elite athlete evidence-based knowledge and preparation for competing in the heat.pdf

paper.citation: Esh CJ, Carter S, Galan-Lopez N, Garrandes F, Bermon S, Adami PE, et al. A review of elite athlete evidence-based knowledge and preparation for competing in the heat. Journal of Science in Sport and Exercise. 2024.
paper.abstract: Review of how elite athletes prepare for competition in heat, covering heat acclimation or acclimatisation, pre-cooling, mid-competition cooling and hydration, and the knowledge behind these choices. The authors report that adoption of heat acclimation has increased since 2015 but is not universal, that cost and access are the main barriers, and that most research covers small samples of elite endurance athletes. They call for regularly updated, multilingual guidance and more research across sports.
paper.tldr: Heat acclimation adoption among elite athletes rose from 15% in 2015 to around 57% to 63% in later championships but is not universal. Cooling and hydration are widely used, so athletes should complete acclimation where possible and use cooling and hydration as complements, not substitutes.
paper.methods: Narrative review of elite athlete heat preparation research, including survey data from five championship events (532 of 9,001 athletes surveyed) and one knowledge survey of athletes and practitioners. The recommendations were drafted by the authors, refined through three rounds of author revision and checked against cited guidelines. No systematic search or formal quality appraisal is described.
paper.findings: Dedicated heat acclimation adoption among surveyed athletes was 15% at Beijing 2015, 63% at Doha 2019 and 57% at Muscat 2022, and barriers included cost and access to hot environments. At Doha 2019, acclimated athletes finished higher (mean position 18th vs 28th, P = 0.009), but their percentage of personal best time was similar (112.6% vs 113.3%), and heat-related medical events were 19% vs 32%, not statistically significant. Pre-planned cooling was used by 50% to 80% of athletes and pre-planned fluid intake by 80% or more, while in one survey 75% to 91% of respondents had never measured core temperature.
paper.limitations: Survey samples are small and self-reported, and they cover only about 6% of competing athletes, mostly endurance athletes at major events. The authors note that competition factors such as pacing and non-heat illness may confound the performance and medical-event comparisons, and that the surveys lack standardisation. The IAAF Beijing 2015 sample is listed as 207 surveyed athletes in Table 1 but n = 307 in Tables 2 and 5.
paper.practicalImplications: Where time allows, plan 10 to 14 consecutive days of active heat exposure (core temperature of 38.5 C or higher, sweating for at least 60 minutes) in conditions similar to or hotter than the competition. If that is not possible, the authors suggest post-exercise sauna (80 C or higher) or hot water immersion (40 C or higher) for 20 to 40 minutes, or extra clothing in training, with supervision and temperature monitoring. Use pre-cooling to complement acclimation rather than replace it, and begin hydration planning days before competition.
paper.athleteDev: The performance evidence is observational: acclimated athletes at Doha 2019 finished higher but did not differ on percentage of personal best time, so the data support planning for heat acclimation rather than predicting race outcome. Plan pre-cooling and fluid strategies in training so they are tested before competition.
paper.rtp: The review covers competition preparation in heat and heat-illness risk, not return to sport after injury or illness. Its exertional heat illness data should not be used to judge when an athlete who has had heat illness can safely return to training or competition.

records.sourceFile: A review on the mechanisms of blood flow restriction     resistance training induced muscle hypertrophy.pdf

paper.citation: Pearson SJ, Hussain SR. A review on the mechanisms of blood-flow restriction resistance training-induced muscle hypertrophy. Sports Medicine. 2014.
paper.abstract: Review of how low-intensity resistance training with blood flow restriction (BFR) produces muscle growth, comparing the roles of mechanical tension and metabolic stress. The authors argue that metabolic stress probably plays the dominant role, with mechanical tension and the downstream mechanisms it triggers contributing, but that the relative contribution of each mechanism is still unclear.
paper.tldr: The authors argue that low-load BFR training builds muscle mainly through metabolic stress, with mechanical tension likely adding to the effect. The mechanisms are not settled, so treat the model as a working hypothesis.
paper.methods: Narrative review of the mechanisms of BFR-induced hypertrophy, with a PubMed search from January 2000 to June 2014 using terms on occlusion, hypertrophy, metabolic stress and mechanical loading, plus reference-list checks. The review groups mechanisms into primary (mechanical tension, metabolic stress) and secondary (fibre recruitment, damage, hormones, cell swelling, reactive oxygen species, nitric oxide, heat shock proteins) and then autocrine and paracrine actions. No formal quality appraisal is described.
paper.findings: The authors report that low-intensity training (about 30 to 50% of 1RM) with BFR at about 110 to 200 mmHg increased muscle size more than the same training without restriction in several cited studies. They argue that metabolic stress is the dominant primary driver, citing a conventional (non-BFR) study at 75% of 1RM in which a no-rest protocol increased muscle size where a with-rest protocol did not, and links between metabolite levels and hypertrophy. They also note that tension-linked mechanisms such as fast-twitch recruitment and reactive oxygen species appear less activated at low loads, so their role under BFR is uncertain.
paper.limitations: The authors state that the relative contribution of each mechanism under BFR is largely unknown, and that mechanical tension and metabolic stress occur together, which makes causal attribution hard. Much of the proposed pathway evidence comes from acute, animal or in vitro studies, and the proposed role of moderate-intensity training is speculative. The search was limited to PubMed and ends in 2014.
paper.practicalImplications: Low-load BFR training is a reasonable option for muscle growth when heavy loads are not suitable, as the cited studies show growth at around 20 to 50% of 1RM with restriction. The authors speculate that moderate loads may combine metabolic stress and mechanical tension best, but this is a hypothesis from their model rather than a tested comparison. Cuff pressure and load should be matched to the study protocols the authors cite rather than to general rules.
paper.athleteDev: Low-load BFR can increase muscle size in the cited studies, but the review does not compare it with heavy training for strength, power or sport performance. Do not use it to predict strength or power gains.
paper.rtp: The review covers hypertrophy mechanisms in healthy training, not rehabilitation after injury or return to sport. Its brief mentions of clinical and rehabilitation settings do not establish load, cuff pressure or safety for injured athletes.

records.sourceFile: A sled push stimulus potentiates        subsequent 20-m sprint performance.pdf

paper.citation: Seitz LB, Mina MA, Haff GG. A sled push stimulus potentiates subsequent 20-m sprint performance. Journal of Science and Medicine in Sport. 2017;20:781-785.
paper.abstract: Twenty rugby league players completed a randomized crossover study in which one sled push, loaded at 75% or 125% body mass, preceded unresisted 20 m sprints at 15 s, 4, 8 and 12 min. After the 75% push, sprints were faster at 4, 8 and 12 min (significant at 8 and 12 min); after the 125% push, sprints were slower at every time point (significant at 15 s and 4 min).
paper.tldr: A single sled push at 75% body mass may speed a 20 m sprint 4 to 12 minutes later, but the effect was small and not every player responded. A push at 125% body mass slowed sprints in this group.
paper.methods: Twenty rugby league players completed one familiarization session and two randomized testing sessions a week apart. Each session had baseline 20 m sprints, a sled push at 75% or 125% body mass, and 20 m sprints at 15 s, 4, 8 and 12 min after the push, compared against each player's fastest baseline sprint.
paper.findings: After the 75% push, sprint time was 0.26 +/- 1.03% slower at 15 s (p = 0.91) and 0.95 +/- 2.00%, 1.80 +/- 1.43% and 1.55 +/- 1.54% faster at 4, 8 and 12 min (ES -0.22, -0.42 and -0.36); only the 8 min (p = 0.001) and 12 min (p = 0.003) changes were significant, and the 4 min change was rated only possibly beneficial. After the 125% push, sprints were slower at all time points (ES 0.34 to 0.64), with Table 1 marking 15 s and 4 min as significantly slower than baseline. The between-condition differences were significant at every time point, large at 15 s (d = -1.07) and very large at 4, 8 and 12 min.
paper.limitations: No control session without a sled push was included (the authors note a fourth session was not feasible), and the sample was 20 players. The authors report that 35% to 70% of players improved after the 75% push, depending on time point. Values differ slightly between sections: the abstract gives -1.54% at 12 min while the results give -1.55%, and the Discussion gives the 125% range as 1.36 to 2.57% (ES 0.38 to 0.67) while the abstract and Table 1 give up to 2.59% (ES 0.34 to 0.64).
paper.practicalImplications: Coaches who use a sled push to prime sprint speed should pay attention to load: in this study 75% body mass was followed by faster sprints and 125% body mass by slower sprints. The faster sprints were seen 4 to 12 minutes after the push, and some players did not respond.
paper.athleteDev: Coaches could try a sled push at about 75% body mass followed by 4 to 12 minutes of rest before maximal 20 m sprints, but the gains were small and not every player responded. Avoid the 125% load before speed work, because sprints were slower after it in this group.
paper.rtp: This study tested sprint times in players after sled pushes and did not include injured players or return-to-sport outcomes, so it cannot inform return-to-sport decisions.

records.sourceFile: Acute effects of cannabis consumption on exercise performance - A systematic and umbrella review.pdf

paper.citation: Charron J, Carey V, Marcotte L'Heureux V, Roy P, Comtois AS, Ferland PM. Acute Effects of Cannabis Consumption on Exercise Performance - A Systematic and Umbrella Review. The Journal of Sports Medicine and Physical Fitness. 2020.
paper.abstract: A systematic and umbrella review of acute cannabis use and exercise performance, covering 8 original studies and 10 reviews. The authors conclude that cannabis before exercise has an ergolytic effect, reducing the ability to maintain effort and work capacity, raising heart and breathing rate and myocardial oxygen demand, and increasing sway in balance tests.
paper.tldr: Acute cannabis use before exercise is reported to reduce work capacity, raise heart rate and worsen balance. The direct evidence is small, dated and heterogeneous, so it should not be treated as settled athlete-specific evidence.
paper.methods: PRISMA-based search of PubMed, Scopus and SPORTDiscus (September 2019) with a manual reference search, selection repeated by a second author, a modified Downs and Black quality rating, and a random-effects inverse-variance meta-analysis of heart rate, systolic and diastolic blood pressure in RevMan 5.4.
paper.findings: In the included studies, cannabis before exercise was associated with lower effort tolerance and maximal and physical work capacity, higher heart rate and rate-pressure product, and more sway in balance tests; individual studies were mixed on blood pressure (3 increased, 2 decreased, 1 no effect). The authors describe the pooled analysis as higher heart rate and blood pressure after cannabis, and 4 of the 10 reviews concluded cannabis is ergolytic, conclusions the authors judge to rest on limited data.
paper.limitations: The authors note heterogeneity in THC dose (7.5 to 50.6 mg), timing (10 to 210 minutes) and participant type, and that most included studies used lower historical THC doses than current products. The Downs and Black power domain scored 1 of 8 and external validity 0 of 16, and the search was run in September 2019, so newer studies are not covered.
paper.practicalImplications: The authors conclude that cannabis should be avoided before exercise to maximise performance. They also state that future studies should use modern THC doses (150 mg) and examine chronic effects, since current evidence does not cover those conditions.
paper.athleteDev: The review supports education that acute cannabis use before training or competition is a performance risk, through effects on effort tolerance, work capacity, heart rate and balance. It does not quantify the effect in trained athletes at current THC doses.
paper.rtp: The review cannot inform return to sport, since it addresses acute performance effects in volunteers, cannabis users and cardiac patients and does not study injured athletes or rehabilitation.

records.sourceFile: Acute impact of Nordic hamstring exercise on sprint performance after 24, 48 and 72 hours.pdf

paper.citation: Alonso-Fernandez D, Lopez-Barreiro J, Garganta R, Taboada-Iglesias Y. Acute impact of Nordic hamstring exercise on sprint performance after 24, 48 and 72 hours. Sports Biomechanics. 2021.
paper.abstract: Twenty-four men were randomly allocated to a Nordic hamstring exercise session group or a no-session control, and 30 m sprint variables were measured at baseline and 24, 48 and 72 h later. The authors report a short-lived fall in high-speed force and maximum speed in the exercise group.
paper.tldr: One session of Nordic hamstring exercise temporarily reduced high-speed sprint force and top speed for up to 48 h in previously unexposed men, with recovery by 72 h. The control group did not change and no between-group difference was significant, so the window is a within-group finding.
paper.methods: Participants were randomised to an experimental group (4 sets of 10 partner-assisted eccentric NHE repetitions) or a control group. A manual radar measured 30 m sprints (mean of three) and derived F0, V0, Pmax, RFmax, Drf and maximum speed by linear regression; analysis used mixed repeated-measures ANOVA with Bonferroni post-hoc tests, and soreness and recovery were rated on a 1 to 10 scale.
paper.findings: In the experimental group, V0 fell 3.4% at 48 h (P = 0.0001), maximum speed fell 2.0% at 24 h and 3.2% at 48 h, and Pmax fell 5.0% at 24 h (P = 0.027), with no change for these outcomes at 72 h. F0, RFmax and Drf did not change, soreness and perceived recovery were unaffected, and no between-group difference was significant at any time point.
paper.limitations: The sample was 24 men with no eccentric NHE experience, studied across a single session, so findings may not apply to conditioned athletes or weekly programmes. Soreness was self-reported in one group only, no damage markers were taken, and the authors note that lower-volume NHE protocols, now common, may give different results.
paper.practicalImplications: The authors suggest leaving about 72 h between a high-volume NHE session and high-speed sprint or competition sessions, at least until athletes are conditioned to the exercise. This rests on within-group changes that returned to baseline by 72 h rather than on a significant between-group effect.
paper.athleteDev: In unconditioned men, sprint force at high speed and top speed were reduced for up to 48 h after one NHE session, so NHE sessions may be best scheduled away from high-speed training or competition until athletes are conditioned. Effects on F0 and soreness were absent.
paper.rtp: The study cannot set a return-to-sport timeline, since it tested healthy unexposed men rather than injured players. The authors' link between reduced sprint performance and hamstring injury risk is drawn from the literature and was not tested here.

records.sourceFile: Addressing muscle-tendon imbalances in adult male athletes with personalized exercise prescription based on tendon strain.pdf

paper.citation: Weidlich K, Domroes T, Bohm S, Arampatzis A, Mersmann F. Addressing muscle-tendon imbalances in adult male athletes with personalized exercise prescription based on tendon strain. European Journal of Applied Physiology. 2024.
paper.abstract: A season-long controlled study of adult male volleyball players compared a personalised tendon-strain loading program with usual training. Knee extensor strength, patellar tendon stiffness and strain, and tendon micromorphology were measured at four time points.
paper.tldr: Individually calibrated isometric loading kept patellar tendon strain stable over a volleyball season, while strain rose in control players on usual training. Strength gains were similar in both groups, and injuries were not measured.
paper.methods: Two teams from one division. The intervention team trained three times a week with isometric knee-extension loads set to 4.5 to 6.5% tendon strain, adjusted every 2 weeks from maximal voluntary contraction tests. Knee extensor moment, tendon force, stiffness, maximum strain and ultrasound peak spatial frequency were measured at four time points and analysed with linear mixed-effects models.
paper.findings: Control players' maximum tendon strain rose, and the share at 9% or more went from 18% at baseline to 80% at M3 and 64% at M4, while in the intervention group it stayed around 38% and strain fluctuations fell. In the intervention group, players with higher baseline strain showed larger strain reductions (r = -0.80) and larger stiffness gains (r = 0.72). Knee extensor strength rose about 8.2% in controls and 6.8% in the intervention group with no interaction, normalised stiffness showed only a trend in the intervention group (P = 0.051), and tendon micromorphology did not change in either group.
paper.limitations: Allocation was by team, not random, measurement intervals differed between groups, and other training content could not be controlled. Dropout was higher than planned, the authors say power may be too low for some interactions, and Table 1 lists 11 control players at M2 although the text reports missing control data only at M1, M3 and M4. No injury outcomes were recorded, and the authors note the added benefit over non-personalised loading is not established.
paper.practicalImplications: The authors suggest individualised loading can limit increases in tendon strain across a season, which may matter for overuse risk in players with high strain. This is a plausible prevention target rather than a demonstrated injury reduction, and the added benefit over non-personalised loading is not yet established.
paper.athleteDev: Staff could use maximal-contraction tendon strain testing to flag players whose strain is rising and consider individualised isometric loads to hold it within 4.5 to 6.5%. The study shows this kept strain stable in the intervention team, but strength gains were not larger than with usual training.
paper.rtp: The study does not establish return-to-sport criteria or rehabilitation progression, since it followed in-season players, a few of whom were symptomatic (VISA-P 87 or below), rather than injured athletes in rehabilitation. Symptom counts did not change systematically in either group.

records.sourceFile: Ammonia inhalants - Use, misue, and role in sports performance.pdf

paper.citation: Bender JM, Popkin CA. Ammonia Inhalants: Use, Misuse, and Role in Sports Performance. Sports Health. 2023.
paper.abstract: This narrative clinical review covers the use, misuse and physiology of ammonia inhalants (smelling salts) in sport. The authors searched MEDLINE and Google Scholar and report that acute inhalation raises heart rate and cerebral blood flow velocity without changing blood pressure. They conclude that ergogenic evidence is limited and inconsistent, and that ammonia inhalants have no role in medical management of head injury.
paper.tldr: Ammonia inhalants have no role in managing a suspected head injury, and their performance benefit is unproven. The only positive signal the review highlights is one small study of repeated Wingate efforts; across single maximal efforts the results were mixed, with one study showing higher rate of force development and others showing no change.
paper.methods: Narrative review of MEDLINE and Google Scholar records using terms including smelling salts, ammonia inhalants, strength, performance, head injury and concussion. The paper summarizes six performance studies in tables and text, along with physiology, historical use and adverse-effect reports. It does not describe a systematic selection process or appraisal of study quality.
paper.findings: Perry et al (15 resistance-trained men) found higher heart rate and middle cerebral artery blood flow velocity after inhalation, with mean arterial pressure unchanged and no change in maximal mid-thigh pull force. Bartolomei et al (20 men) reported higher peak rate of force development, but not countermovement jump power or maximal force. Rogers et al (12 active women) found higher mean and peak power over three repeated Wingate tests, with no change in heart rate or fatigue index. Richmond et al, Vigil et al and Campbell et al found no gain in repetitions, deadlift one-repetition maximum or most functional markers, although Campbell et al found higher heart rate, alertness and perceived performance.
paper.limitations: The review is narrative and does not report how many studies were screened. Most cited studies are small (12 to 25 participants) and mostly male, and the authors note that their results conflict. Safety conclusions rest on case reports, mechanistic reasoning and historical exposure data rather than controlled trials.
paper.practicalImplications: Do not use ammonia inhalants to assess or manage a suspected concussion or head injury, because they can mask symptoms and the withdrawal reflex may worsen a head or neck injury. Do not present them as a proven performance aid, since benefits are small or unconfirmed. Staff should be aware that a severe allergic reaction has been reported in one case report, and the authors theorize a possible syncope risk during heavy upright lifting.
paper.athleteDev: The performance evidence is limited and inconsistent, so ammonia inhalants should not be relied on to improve strength or power. The most consistent possible effect is on repeated high-intensity efforts, shown in one study of women, while single maximal efforts showed no benefit for most measures.
paper.rtp: Ammonia inhalants have no role in return-to-play decisions or in managing a head injury. They can mask concussion symptoms and may encourage continued participation, so this paper cannot support any use of inhalants in return-to-sport clearance.

records.sourceFile: Ankle and plantar flexor muscle-tendon unit function in sprinters - A narrative review.pdf

paper.citation: Crotty ED, Furlong LAM, Harrison AJ. Ankle and Plantar Flexor Muscle-Tendon Unit Function in Sprinters: A Narrative Review. Sports Med. 2023.
paper.abstract: Narrative review of ankle joint and plantar flexor muscle-tendon unit (MTU) function across the sprint start, acceleration and maximum velocity phases, and of the musculotendinous properties linked to plantar flexor performance. The authors describe the ankle as most critical during acceleration and as a net energy dissipater at maximum velocity, and they state that an optimal plantar flexor MTU profile potentially exists.
paper.tldr: The ankle and plantar flexor MTU matter most at the sprint start and during acceleration, when rear-leg ankle function and push-off force are key. At top speed the ankle mainly absorbs energy and transfers it up the chain, and the muscle and tendon traits that make a faster sprinter are still unclear.
paper.methods: Narrative review. One author screened titles and abstracts from PubMed and Google Scholar searches (212 records; 84 full texts; 31 excluded, mainly because participants were not sprinters). In total 53 articles were included, plus 12 from reference lists, for 65 studies. No formal quality appraisal is reported.
paper.findings: Sprint start: the rear-leg ankle is an important contributor, and in one cited comparison elite Jamaican sprinters had a higher rate of force development than national-level sprinters (259 vs 175 N/kg/s). Acceleration: the ankle contributes about 15% of positive work in the first stance and 38-48% in the second stance, per the cited studies. Maximum velocity: the ankle is a net energy dissipater, with peak plantar flexor power larger in the negative work phase (-4930 W) than in the positive work phase (3954 W) in one cited study. Muscle roles: based on simulation, the soleus acts mainly as a supporter and the gastrocnemius as both an accelerator and a supporter. Longer gastrocnemius fascicles correlated with faster 100 m personal bests (r about -0.29 to -0.57 with PB time in cited studies), while results for muscle size and tendon stiffness are inconsistent.
paper.limitations: Most included studies have small samples and single-subject, cross-sectional or simulation designs, and the sprinters studied are mainly male. The authors flag a lack of research on female athletes and truly world-class sprinters, and note that model-derived fascicle and tendon values depend on model assumptions.
paper.practicalImplications: The review links rear-leg ankle and plantar flexor force production to block power and early acceleration, so these qualities are a reasonable focus for sprint-start work. Block inclination above about 65 degrees may place the plantar flexor MTU at an unfavorable part of its length-tension curve, according to the cited studies. Do not set a single muscle size or tendon stiffness value as a target, because the review says the optimal profile is not yet defined.
paper.athleteDev: Use the review's phase framework to decide where ankle and plantar flexor work fits: sprint start and early acceleration first. Track fascicle or tendon measures only where they can be tied to sprint outcomes, since the review finds those links inconsistent.
paper.rtp: The review covers healthy sprint mechanics and does not address injury, rehabilitation or return to sport, so it cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. It offers no tendon or muscle criteria for clearing an athlete to sprint.

records.sourceFile: Application of velocity loss thresholds during free weight resistance training Responses and reproducibility of perceptual, metabolic, and neuromuscular outcomes.pdf

paper.citation: Weakley J, McLaren S, Ramirez-Lopez C, García-Ramos A, Dalton-Barron N, Banyard H, et al. Application of velocity loss thresholds during free-weight resistance training: Responses and reproducibility of perceptual, metabolic, and neuromuscular outcomes. Journal of Sports Sciences. 2020;38(5):477-485.
paper.abstract: Twelve male team-sport athletes completed five sets of barbell back squats at about 0.70 m/s, with sets stopped at 10%, 20% or 30% velocity loss on separate days. Post-set dRPE and blood lactate rose with the threshold, and CMJ variables fell, and the four-week variability of each response is reported as an SD.
paper.tldr: In 12 male university rugby players, higher velocity loss thresholds in the back squat produced greater perceived effort, lactate and post-set jump losses within a session. The authors report small four-week variability in these responses, though some variability estimates were imprecise.
paper.methods: Repeated, counterbalanced crossover design. Twelve male rugby athletes performed five sets of barbell back squats at a starting mean concentric velocity of 0.70 +/- 0.01 m/s, with sets ended at 10%, 20% or 30% velocity loss. Each protocol was completed twice, four weeks apart, and dRPE, blood lactate and CMJ were measured after each set and analysed with linear mixed models.
paper.findings: Between protocols, dRPE and blood lactate increased with the threshold (30% > 20% > 10%); lactate was 1.7 mmol/L higher for 20% vs 10% and 3.6 mmol/L higher for 30% vs 10%. CMJ height was lower at greater thresholds by small amounts (-1.9 cm for 20% vs 10%, -3.4 cm for 30% vs 10%), but impulse differences for 20% vs 10% and 30% vs 20% were likely trivial and the PPO difference for 30% vs 20% was possibly trivial. The four-week SDs were dRPE 8-11 au, B[La] 0.8-1.0 mmol/L, CMJ height 1.6-2.0 cm, CMJ peak relative power 1.0-1.8 W/kg, CMJ peak velocity 0.04-0.06 m/s and CMJ impulse at 100 ms 5.7-11.9 N s.
paper.limitations: The sample was 12 male rugby players performing one exercise at a fixed starting velocity of 0.70 m/s, so results may not transfer to other athletes, lifts or starting velocities. Responses at 24 hours were not measured, training and lifestyle were not controlled between test occasions, and inferences used magnitude-based decisions. Several four-week SD confidence intervals for the 10% condition cross zero (for example B[La] 0.8, 90% CI -0.2 to 1.2), and one Table 1 interval is misprinted (RPE-B 30 vs 10%: 27; 23).
paper.practicalImplications: Velocity loss thresholds give staff a way to set the internal response to a set: 30% produced more perceived effort and lactate, and larger jump losses, than 10%. The authors suggest 10% during congested periods or close to competition, and 30% for hypertrophy and strength endurance blocks. Staff should record the starting velocity in the warm-up and the first repetition of each set, since the protocol depends on it.
paper.athleteDev: Velocity loss thresholds can set the within-session effort and fatigue for a squat session, with 30% giving more perceived exertion, lactate and CMJ loss than 10%. Choose the threshold to match the training goal, such as 10% for lower-fatigue blocks and 30% for hypertrophy or strength endurance work. The findings were from a single exercise with a fixed starting velocity of 0.70 m/s.
paper.rtp: This study cannot inform return to sport. It tested healthy male athletes in the off-season and did not include injured athletes, rehabilitation or readiness to return.
